content: Didymium, derived from the Greek word meaning twin element, is a mixture of the elements praseodymium and neodymium. It is commonly used in safety glasses for glassblowing and blacksmithing, particularly when a propane-powered forge is employed. These glasses filter out the yellowish light emitted by hot sodium in the glass without impairing general vision, unlike the dark lenses used in welder's glasses. Additionally, didymium glasses block the intense ultraviolet light emitted by superheated forge gases and the insulation lining the forge walls, thereby protecting the eyes of craftsmen from significant cumulative damage. This protection is crucial in preventing conditions such as arc eye, also known as welder's flash or photokeratitis. Didymium photographic filters are often utilized to enhance the vibrancy of autumn scenery by making leaves appear more vivid. This effect is achieved through the material's unique properties, which selectively remove part of the orange region of the color spectrum. The presence of these orange hues can otherwise make certain elements of an image appear muddy. Didymium is also employed in calibration materials. Didymium was first identified by Carl Mosander in 1841. He named it didymium due to its similarity to lanthanum, with which it was found. Mosander mistakenly believed didymium to be a single element, under the impression that ceria (sometimes referred to as cerite), isolated by Jöns Jakob Berzelius in 1803, was a mixture of cerium, lanthanum, and didymium. While Mosander correctly identified lanthanum as an element, he was incorrect about didymium. His work was impressive for the time, as spectroscopy had not yet been invented. His three elements accounted for at least 95% of the rare earths in the original cerite from Bastnäs, Sweden. The name didymium may have been a playful reference to the fact that Mosander's four children were born as two sets of twins. Didymium was not difficult to identify, as it imparted a pinkish hue to the salts of ceria in their trivalent form. The real challenge lay in isolating the colorless lanthanum from the mixture. During the period when didymium was believed to be an element, it was assigned the symbol Di. In 1885, Carl Auer von Welsbach successfully separated the salts of praseodymium and neodymium through fractional crystallization of their double ammonium nitrates from nitric acid. He initially proposed naming the two elements praseodidymium (green didymium) and neodidymium (new didymium), but the names were later shortened to praseodymium and neodymium. The term didymium persisted in its unaltered form, partly due to its use in glassblowers' goggles. During World War I, didymium glass was reportedly used to transmit Morse code across battlefields. The glass did not absorb enough light to make variations in lamp intensity obvious, but observers with binoculars equipped with prisms could detect the absorption bands flashing on and off. The name didymium also endured in the rare earth industry. In the United States, commercial didymium salts referred to the material remaining after cerium was removed from the natural abundance mixture obtained from monazite. These salts contained lanthanum as well as Mosander's didymium. A typical composition might include 46% lanthanum, 34% neodymium, 11% praseodymium, with the remainder mostly samarium and gadolinium, for material extracted from South African monazite (e.g., from Steenkampskraal). European usage was closer to Mosander's original composition. Such cerium-depleted light lanthanide mixtures have been widely used in the production of petroleum-cracking catalysts. The ratio of praseodymium to neodymium in didymium varies depending on the source but is often around 1:3, with neodymium always dominating. This dominance is why neodymium was given the neo designation, as it is responsible for most of the color in the salts of the old element. In ores, neodymium is relatively more abundant in monazite compared to bastnäsite compositions. This difference is noticeable when unseparated mixtures derived from each source are compared side by side: monazite-derived products tend to have a pinkish hue, while bastnäsite-derived products are more brownish due to the latter's higher relative praseodymium content. The original cerite from Bastnäs has a rare earth composition similar to that of monazite sand. In the late 1920s, Leo Moser recombined praseodymium and neodymium in a 1:1 ratio to create Heliolite glass, which exhibits color-changing properties, shifting between amber, reddish, and green depending on the light source. More recently, it was discovered that praseodymium could be incorporated into the composition of neodymium-iron-boron magnets without significantly compromising magnetic strength. This innovation helps stretch the neodymium supply while providing a use for the underutilized praseodymium. For such magnets, the appropriate mixture can be prepared directly through solvent extraction without the need to purify either component separately.
